metadata.title: Multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund analysis and connexion to Bochner-Riesz multipliers

nodes.name: H\"ormander's condition
nodes.statement: $$ | \partial^\alpha m(\xi)| \lesssim |\xi|^{-|\alpha|}=d(\xi,0)^{-|\alpha|},$$
nodes.statement_short: Symbol derivative decay measured against the single frequency $0$.

nodes.name: Multi-frequency H\"ormander condition
nodes.statement: $$ | \partial^\alpha m(\xi)| \lesssim d(\xi,\Theta)^{-|\alpha|},$$ with $d(\xi,\Theta):= \min_{1\leq i \leq N} |\xi-\xi_i|$.
nodes.statement_short: Symbol derivative decay measured against the distance to a whole collection $\Theta$ of frequencies.

nodes.name: Calder\'on-Zygmund operator relatively to $\Theta$ (multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator)
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta:=(\xi_1,...,\xi_N)$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies of $\R^n$. An $L^2$-bounded linear operator $T$ is said to be a Calder\'on-Zygmund operator relatively to $\Theta$ if there exist operators $(T_j)_{j=1,...,N}$ and kernels $(K_j)_{j=1,...,N}$ verifying \begin{itemize} \item Decomposition: $T=\sum_{j=1}^N T_j$; \item Integral representation of $T_j$: for every function $f\in L^2$ compactly supported and $x\in \textrm{supp}(f)^{c}$, $$ T_j(f)(x) = \int K_j(x,y) f(y);$$ \item Regularity of the modulated kernels: for every $x\neq y$ $$ \sum_{j=1}^N \left|\nabla_{(x,y)}\ e^{i\xi_j\cdot(x-y)} K_j(x,y)\right| \lesssim |x-y|^{-n-1}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: An $L^2$-bounded operator splitting as $\sum_j T_j$ whose kernels, after modulation by $e^{i\xi_j\cdot(x-y)}$, jointly satisfy the standard Calder\'on-Zygmund gradient bound.
differentia: Integral representation of $T_j$: for every function $f\in L^2$ compactly supported and $x\in \textrm{supp}(f)^{c}$, $$ T_j(f)(x) = \int K_j(x,y) f(y);$$
Regularity of the modulated kernels: for every $x\neq y$ $$ \sum_{j=1}^N \left|\nabla_{(x,y)}\ e^{i\xi_j\cdot(x-y)} K_j(x,y)\right| \lesssim |x-y|^{-n-1}.$$

nodes.name: Weakening to $\epsilon$-H\"older regularity
nodes.statement: As usual, we can weaken the regularity assumption and just require an $\epsilon$-H\"older regularity on the modulated kernels.

nodes.name: Orthogonal decomposition and the trivial bound of order $N$
nodes.statement: If the decomposition is assumed to be orthogonal (which means that for $i\neq j$, $T_iT_j^*=0$) then it follows that each operator $T_j$ is a modulated Calder\'on-Zygmund operator. Such a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator can also be pointwisely bounded by a sum of $N$ modulated (classical) Calder\'on-Zygmund operators and have the same boundedness properties with an implicit constant of order $N$. The aim is to study how this order can be improved using sharp estimates.
nodes.statement_short: Under orthogonality the trivial bound is of order $N$; the goal of the paper is to improve that order.

nodes.name: Unweighted $L^p$ and weak-type $(1,1)$ bounds for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies and $T$ an associated multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator. Then \begin{itemize} \item for $p\in(1,\infty)$, $T$ is bounded on $L^p$ with $$ \|T\|_{L^p \to L^p} \lesssim N^{\left|\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\right|}.$$ \item for $p=1$, $T$ is of weak-type $(1,1)$ with $$ \|T\|_{L^1 \to L^{1,\infty}} \lesssim N^{\frac{1}{2}}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators obey $L^p$ bounds growing like $N^{|1/p-1/2|}$ and a weak $(1,1)$ bound of order $\sqrt{N}$.
assumptions: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies
conclusions: $T$ is bounded on $L^p$ with $$ \|T\|_{L^p \to L^p} \lesssim N^{\left|\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\right|}.$$
$T$ is of weak-type $(1,1)$ with $$ \|T\|_{L^1 \to L^{1,\infty}} \lesssim N^{\frac{1}{2}}.$$

nodes.name: Optimality of the constant $N^{1/2}$
nodes.statement: This theorem relies on an adapted Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition introduced in \cite{NOT} by Nazarov, Oberlin and Thiele. We point out that there the constant $N^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is shown to be optimal and this is the same for the previous weak-type estimate.
nodes.statement_short: The theorem rests on the [NOT] decomposition, whose $\sqrt{N}$ constant is known to be optimal.

nodes.name: Weighted boundedness of linear Calder\'on-Zygmund operators on $L^p(\omega)$, $\omega\in{\mathbb A}_p$
nodes.statement: linear Calder\'on-Zygmund operators are bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ for $p\in(1,\infty)$ and every weight $\omega$ belonging to the Muckenhoupt's class ${\mathbb A}_p$
assumptions: every weight $\omega$ belonging to the Muckenhoupt's class ${\mathbb A}_p$
conclusions: linear Calder\'on-Zygmund operators are bounded on $L^p(\omega)$

nodes.name: Johnson-Neugebauer characterisation of ${\mathbb A}_r \cap RH_s$
nodes.statement: From \cite{JN}, we know that for $r,s>1$, $$ {\mathbb A}_{r} \cap RH_s = \left\{\omega, \omega^{s} \in{\mathbb A}_{1+s(r-1)}\right\},$$ so these classes of weights are equivalent to a class of powers of Muckenhoupt's weights.
nodes.statement_short: Intersecting ${\mathbb A}_r$ with a reverse H\"older class is the same as asking a power of the weight to be Muckenhoupt.
conclusions: $$ {\mathbb A}_{r} \cap RH_s = \left\{\omega, \omega^{s} \in{\mathbb A}_{1+s(r-1)}\right\},$$

nodes.name: Weight class ${\mathcal W}^p (p_0 , q_0 )$
nodes.statement: weights belonging to the class ${\mathcal W}^p (p_0 , q_0 ) := {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{p_0}} \cap RH_{(\frac{q_0}{p})'}$ for some exponents $p_0<q_0$

nodes.name: Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies. For $p\in (1,\infty)$, $s\in(1,p)$ and $t\in(1,\infty)$, then every multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator $T$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ for every weight $\omega \in RH_{t'} \cap {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$ with $$ \|T\|_{L^p(\omega) \to L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{\gamma}$$ and $$ \gamma:=\frac{tp}{s\min\{2,s\}}+\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right|.$$ We emphasize that this result is only interesting when $\gamma<1$.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted $L^p(\omega)$ boundedness with constant $N^\gamma$ for weights in $RH_{t'}\cap{\mathbb A}_{p/s}$, useful only when $\gamma<1$.
assumptions: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies
conclusions: $T$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$
$$ \|T\|_{L^p(\omega) \to L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{\gamma}$$ and $$ \gamma:=\frac{tp}{s\min\{2,s\}}+\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right|.$$

nodes.name: Average of $f$ on a set $E$
nodes.statement: For a subset $E\subset \rn$ of finite and non-vanishing measure and $f$ a locally integrable function, the average of $f$ on $E$ is defined by $$ \aver{E} f dx := \frac{1}{|E|}\int_E f(x) dx.$$

nodes.name: Maximal Hardy-Littlewood function $\M$
nodes.statement: Let us denote by ${\mathcal Q}$ the collection of all balls in $\rn$. We write $\M$ for the maximal Hardy-Littlewood function: $$ {\mathcal M} f(x)= \sup_{{\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{Q\in{\mathcal Q}}{x\in Q}}} \aver{Q}|f|dx.$$

nodes.name: $L^p$-averaged maximal function $\M_p$
nodes.statement: For $p\in (1,\infty)$, we set $\M_p f(x)=\M(|f|^p)(x)^{1/p}$.

nodes.name: Nikolskii-type inequality for shift invariant spaces (Borwein-Erd\'elyi lemma)
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta\subset \R^n$ be a finite collection of frequencies and $Q$ be a ball. For every function $\phi$ belonging to the subspace of $L^2(3Q)$, spanned by $(e^{i\xi\cdot})_{\xi\in \Theta}$, we have for $p\in[1,2]$ \begin{equation} \|\phi\|_{L^\infty(Q)} \lesssim (\sharp \Theta)^{\frac{1}{p}} \left(\aver{3Q} |\phi|^p dx \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For exponential-sum functions, the $L^\infty(Q)$ norm is controlled by the $L^p(3Q)$ average with a loss of $(\sharp\Theta)^{1/p}$.
assumptions: Let $\Theta\subset \R^n$ be a finite collection of frequencies and $Q$ be a ball
For every function $\phi$ belonging to the subspace of $L^2(3Q)$, spanned by $(e^{i\xi\cdot})_{\xi\in \Theta}$
conclusions: \begin{equation} \|\phi\|_{L^\infty(Q)} \lesssim (\sharp \Theta)^{\frac{1}{p}} \left(\aver{3Q} |\phi|^p dx \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Extension of the Borwein-Erd\'elyi lemma to several dimensions
nodes.statement: In \cite{BE}, this lemma is stated and proved in a one-dimensional setting. However, the proof only relies on the additive group structure of the ambient space by using translation operators. So the exact same proof can be extended to a multi-dimensional setting.
nodes.statement_short: The one-dimensional proof of the lemma transfers verbatim to $\R^n$ since it only uses translations.

nodes.name: Extension of the multi-frequency Nikolskii lemma to $p\in(2,\infty)$
nodes.statement: The question of extending the previous lemma for $p\in(2,\infty)$ is still open in such a general situation. Of course, (\ref{aze}) is true for $p=\infty$ and so it would be reasonable to expect the result for intermediate exponents $p \in(2,\infty)$. Unfortunately, the well-known interpolation theory does not apply here. \\ However, in some specific situations, we may extend this lemma for $p\geq 2$. Indeed, if $p=2k$ is an even integer then applying (\ref{aze}) with $p=2$ and $\Theta^k:=\{\theta_{i_1}+...+\theta_{i_k},\ \theta_i\in \Theta\}$ to $\phi^k$ yields \begin{align*} \|\phi \|_{L^\infty(Q)} & \lesssim \|\phi^k \|_{L^\infty(Q)}^{\frac{1}{k}} \\ & \lesssim (\sharp \Theta^k )^{\frac{1}{2k}} \left(\aver{3Q} |\phi|^{2k} dx \right)^{\frac{1}{2k}} \\ & \simeq (\sharp \Theta^k )^{\frac{1}{p}} \left(\aver{3Q} |\phi|^{p} dx \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \end{align*} By this way, we see that an extension of (\ref{aze}) for $p\geq 2$ may be related to sharp combinatorial arguments, to estimate $\sharp \Theta^k$ (a trivial bound is $\sharp \Theta^k \leq (\sharp \Theta)^{k}$ which does not improve (\ref{aze})).
nodes.statement_short: Whether the Nikolskii-type lemma holds for $p>2$ is open; even integers reduce it to estimating the sumset size $\sharp\Theta^k$.

nodes.name: Muckenhoupt class ${\mathbb A}_p$
nodes.statement: A weight $\omega$ is a non-negative locally integrable function. We say that a weight $\omega\in {\mathbb A}_p$, $1<p<\infty$, if there exists a positive constant $C$ such that for every ball $Q$, $$\bigg(\aver{Q} \omega\,dx\bigg)\, \bigg(\aver{Q} \omega^{1-p'}\,dx\bigg)^{p-1}\le C. $$ For $p=1$, we say that $\omega\in {\mathbb A}_1$ if there is a positive constant $C$ such that for every ball $Q$, $$ \aver{Q} \omega \,dx \le C\, \omega (y), \qquad \mbox{for a.e. }y\in Q. $$ We write ${\mathbb A}_\infty=\cup_{p\ge 1} {\mathbb A}_p$.
nodes.statement_short: A weight is Muckenhoupt-${\mathbb A}_p$ when the product of the average of $\omega$ and of $\omega^{1-p'}$ over every ball stays bounded.
nodes.genus: A weight $\omega$ is a non-negative locally integrable function
differentia: there exists a positive constant $C$ such that for every ball $Q$, $$\bigg(\aver{Q} \omega\,dx\bigg)\, \bigg(\aver{Q} \omega^{1-p'}\,dx\bigg)^{p-1}\le C. $$

nodes.name: $L^p(\omega)$-boundedness of $\M$ characterises ${\mathbb A}_p$
nodes.statement: for $p\in(1,\infty)$, the maximal function $\M$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ if and only if $\omega \in {\mathbb A}_p$
conclusions: the maximal function $\M$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ if and only if $\omega \in {\mathbb A}_p$

nodes.name: Reverse H\"older class $RH_p$
nodes.statement: A weight $\omega \in RH_p$, $1<p<\infty$, if there is a constant $C$ such that for every ball $Q$, $$ \bigg( \aver{Q} \omega^p\,dx \bigg)^{1/p} \leq C \bigg(\aver{Q} \omega\,dx\bigg). $$ It is well known that ${\mathbb A}_\infty=\cup_{r>1} RH_r$. Thus, for $p=1$ it is understood that $RH_1={\mathbb A}_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: A weight is in $RH_p$ when its $L^p$ average over every ball is comparable to its $L^1$ average.
differentia: there is a constant $C$ such that for every ball $Q$, $$ \bigg( \aver{Q} \omega^p\,dx \bigg)^{1/p} \leq C \bigg(\aver{Q} \omega\,dx\bigg). $$
nodes.origin_citation: classical reverse H\"older classes; Johnson & Neugebauer 1991

nodes.name: Rubio de Francia's Littlewood-Paley inequality for arbitrary intervals
nodes.statement: It is well-known by Rubio de Francia's work \cite{Rubio} that for $q\in(1,2]$, the functional \begin{equation} f \rightarrow \left( \sum_{\omega\in\Delta} \left|{\mathcal F}^{-1}[{\bf 1}_{\omega} {\mathcal F}f]\right|^q \right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \end{equation} is bounded on $L^p$ for $p\in(q',\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\ell^q$-square-function over an arbitrary disjoint family of intervals is $L^p$-bounded for $p>q'$, uniformly in the family.
assumptions: Associated to $\Theta$, we have a collection of disjoint intervals $\Delta:=\{ (-\infty,\xi_1), (\xi_1,\xi_2),...,(\xi_N,\infty)\}$
conclusions: the functional \begin{equation} f \rightarrow \left( \sum_{\omega\in\Delta} \left|{\mathcal F}^{-1}[{\bf 1}_{\omega} {\mathcal F}f]\right|^q \right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \end{equation} is bounded on $L^p$

nodes.name: The multi-frequency Hilbert transform
nodes.statement: As explained in the introduction, an example of such multi-frequency operators in the $1$-dimensional setting is the multi-frequency Hilbert transform. In $\R$, consider an arbitrary collection of frequencies $\Theta:=(\xi_1,...,\xi_N)$ (assumed to be indexed by the increasing order $\xi_1< \xi_2< \cdots < \xi_N$). The associated multi-frequency Hilbert transform is the Fourier multiplier corresponding to the symbol $$ m(\xi) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} -1, & \xi<\xi_1 \\ (-1)^{j+1}, & \xi_j<\xi<\xi_{j+1} \\ (-1)^{N+1}, & \xi>\xi_N. \end{array} \right. $$ Associated to $\Theta$, we have a collection of disjoint intervals $\Delta:=\{ (-\infty,\xi_1), (\xi_1,\xi_2),...,(\xi_N,\infty)\}$. It is well-known by Rubio de Francia's work \cite{Rubio} that for $q\in(1,2]$, the functional \begin{equation} f \rightarrow \left( \sum_{\omega\in\Delta} \left|{\mathcal F}^{-1}[{\bf 1}_{\omega} {\mathcal F}f]\right|^q \right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \end{equation} is bounded on $L^p$ for $p\in(q',\infty)$. The boundedness of the multi-frequency Hilbert transform is closely related to the understanding of (\ref{eq:f}) for $q\to 1$. \mb We point out that in Rubio de Francia's result, the obtained estimates do not depend on the collection of intervals $\Delta$. More precisely, excepted the end-point $p=q'$, the range $(q',\infty)$ is optimal for a uniform (with respect to the collection $\Delta$) $L^p$-boundedness of (\ref{eq:f}). So it is natural that for $q\to 1$ things are more difficult, which is illustrated by our multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund analysis. Indeed, for example if one considers the particular case $\Theta:=(1,...,N)$, then following the notations of Remark \ref{rem:lem}, we have $\Theta^k =\{k,...,kN\}$ and so $\sharp \Theta^k = k(N-1)+1 \simeq k N$. Hence, in this situation we have observed (see Remark \ref{rem:lem}) that we can extend Lemma \ref{lem} to exponents $p\in[1,\infty]$ (the implicit constant appearing in (\ref{aze}) is only depending on $p$). By this way, Theorem \ref{thm:weight} can be improved and we obtain a better exponent $$ \gamma=\frac{tp}{s^2}+\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right|.$$ Consequently, it seems that for the $L^p$-boundedness of the multi-frequency Hilbert transform, the collection $\Theta$ could play an important role (which was not the case for the $\ell^q$-functional (\ref{eq:f}) with $q'<p$).
nodes.statement_short: The sign-alternating multiplier attached to $N$ ordered frequencies; for $\Theta=(1,\dots,N)$ the sumset is small, so the lemma extends to all $p$ and $\gamma$ improves to $tp/s^2+|1/2-1/s|$.

nodes.name: Multi-frequency operators coming from a covering of the frequency space
nodes.statement: Let $(Q_j)_{j=1,...,N}$ be a family of disjoint cubes and $\phi_j$ a smooth function with $\widehat{\phi_j}$ supported and adapted to $Q_j$. Then consider the linear operator given by $$ T(f) = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi_j \ast f.$$ It is easy to check that $T$ is a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator, associated to the collection $\Theta:=(\xi_1,...,\xi_N)$ where for every $j$, $\xi_j:=c(Q_j)$ is the center of the ball $Q_j$. With $r_j$ the radius of $Q_j$, we have the regularity estimate $$ \sum_{j=1}^N \left|\nabla_{(x,y)}\ e^{i\xi_j\cdot(x-y)} \phi_j(x-y)\right| \lesssim |x-y|^{-n-1} \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{(r_j |x-y|)^{n+1}}{(1+r_j|x-y|)^{M}},$$ for every integer $M>0$. So boundedness of $T$ (Theorem \ref{thm:boundedness}) yields the inequality \begin{equation} \left\| \sum_{j=1}^N \phi_j \ast f \right\|_{L^p} \lesssim C(r_1,...,r_N) N^{\left|\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\right|} \|f\|_{L^p}, \end{equation} with $$ C(r_1,...,r_N):= \sup_{t>0} \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{(r_j t)^{n+1}}{(1+r_jt)^{M}}.$$ Let us examine some particular situations: \begin{itemize} \item If the cubes $(Q_j)_j$ have an equal side-length, then as for Proposition \ref{prop}, simple arguments imply (\ref{eq:ex}) for $p\in[1,\infty]$ without the constant $C(r_1,...,r_N)$. \item If the collection $(Q_j)_j$ is dyadic: it exists a point $\xi_0$, $d(Q_j,\xi_0) \simeq r_{Q_j} \simeq 2^j$ then Littlewood-Paley theory implies (\ref{eq:ex}) without the factor $N^{|\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}|}$ (in this case $C(r_1,...,r_N)\simeq 1$). \item If the cubes $(Q_j)$ have only the dyadic scale: $r_{Q_j} \simeq 2^j$ (but no assumptions on the centers of the balls) then Littlewood-Paley theory cannot be used. However, our previous results can be applied in this situation and so (\ref{eq:ex}) holds and $C(r_1,...,r_N) \simeq 1$. \end{itemize} We aim to use the new multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund analysis to extend these inequalities with replacing the convolution operators by more general Calder\'on-Zygmund operators, still satisfying some orthogonality properties.
nodes.statement_short: Sums of convolutions $\sum_j\phi_j\ast f$ with frequency-localized $\phi_j$ are multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators, giving $L^p$ bounds beyond the reach of Littlewood-Paley theory.

nodes.name: Multi-frequency operators coming from variation norm estimates
nodes.statement: As explained in the introduction, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund analysis has been first developed for proving a variation norm variant of a Bourgain's maximal inequality. So our results can be adapted in such a framework. For example, in \cite{GMS} Grafakos, Martell and Soria have studied maximal inequalities of the form $$ \left\| \sup_{j=1,...,N} \left| T( e^{i\theta_j\cdot} f) \right| \right\|_{L^p} \lesssim \|f\|_{L^p}$$ where $(\theta_j)_{j=1,...,N}$ is a collection of frequencies and $T$ a fixed Calder\'on-Zygmund operator. We can ask the same question, for a variation norm variant: for $q\in[1,\infty)$ consider $$ \left(\sum_{j=1}^N \left| T( e^{i\theta_j\cdot} f) \right|^q \right)^{\frac{1}{q}}$$ and study its boundedness on $L^p$, with a sharp control of the behaviour with respect to $N$. By a linearization argument (involving Rademacher's functions), this $\ell^q$-functional can be realized as an average of modulated Calder\'on-Zygmund operators, associated to the collection $\Theta:=(\theta_j)_j$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\ell^q$-variant of the Grafakos-Martell-Soria maximally modulated inequality linearizes into an average of modulated Calder\'on-Zygmund operators.

nodes.name: Weak type $(1,1)$ bound of order $N^{1/2}$
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta=(\xi_1,...,\xi_N)$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies as above and $T$ be a Calder\'on-Zygmund operator relatively to $\Theta$. Then $T$ is of weak type $(1,1)$ with (uniformly with respect to $N$) $$ \|T\|_{L^1\to L^{1,\infty}} \lesssim N^{\frac{1}{2}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: A multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator maps $L^1$ into $L^{1,\infty}$ with norm $O(\sqrt{N})$.
assumptions: Let $\Theta=(\xi_1,...,\xi_N)$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies as above
$T$ be a Calder\'on-Zygmund operator relatively to $\Theta$
conclusions: $T$ is of weak type $(1,1)$ with (uniformly with respect to $N$) $$ \|T\|_{L^1\to L^{1,\infty}} \lesssim N^{\frac{1}{2}}.$$
nodes.section: 2 Unweighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition of Nazarov, Oberlin and Thiele
nodes.statement: we use the Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition\footnote{In \cite{NOT}, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition is only described in $\R$. The proof is a combination of Lemma \ref{lem} and the usual Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition. Since both of them can be extended in a multi-dimensional framework, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition performed in \cite{NOT} still holds in $\R^n$.} of \cite{NOT} related to the collection of frequencies $\Theta$. So the function $f$ can be decomposed $f = g + \sum_{J\in {\bf J}} b_J$ with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item ${\bf J}$ is a collection of balls and $(3J)_{J\in{\bf J}}$ has a bounded overlap; \item for each $J\in{\bf J}$, $b_J$ is supported in $3J$; \item we have \begin{equation} \sum_{J \in{\bf J}} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}; \end{equation} \item the ``good part'' $g$ satisfies \begin{equation} \|g\|_{L^2}^2 \lesssim \|f\|_{L^1} \sqrt{N} \lambda; \end{equation} \item the cubes $J$ satisfy \begin{equation} \|f\|_{L^1(J)} \lesssim |J|\lambda N^{-\frac{1}{2}} , \quad \|f-b_J\|_{L^2(J)} \lesssim \sqrt{|J|} \lambda; \end{equation} \item we have cancellation for all the frequencies of $\Theta$: for all $j=1,...,N$ and $J\in{\bf J}$, $\widehat{b_J}(\xi_j)=0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Any $f\in L^1$ splits as $g+\sum_J b_J$ with $\sqrt{N}$-losses in the size and energy bounds and with $\widehat{b_J}$ vanishing at every frequency of $\Theta$.
assumptions: related to the collection of frequencies $\Theta$
conclusions: the function $f$ can be decomposed $f = g + \sum_{J\in {\bf J}} b_J$
\begin{equation} \sum_{J \in{\bf J}} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}; \end{equation}
\begin{equation} \|g\|_{L^2}^2 \lesssim \|f\|_{L^1} \sqrt{N} \lambda; \end{equation}
we have cancellation for all the frequencies of $\Theta$: for all $j=1,...,N$ and $J\in{\bf J}$, $\widehat{b_J}(\xi_j)=0$.

nodes.name: Proof of the weak type $(1,1)$ bound
nodes.statement: Consider $f$ a function in $L^1$ and $\lambda>0$, we use the Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition\footnote{In \cite{NOT}, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition is only described in $\R$. The proof is a combination of Lemma \ref{lem} and the usual Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition. Since both of them can be extended in a multi-dimensional framework, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition performed in \cite{NOT} still holds in $\R^n$.} of \cite{NOT} related to the collection of frequencies $\Theta$. So the function $f$ can be decomposed $f = g + \sum_{J\in {\bf J}} b_J$ with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item ${\bf J}$ is a collection of balls and $(3J)_{J\in{\bf J}}$ has a bounded overlap; \item for each $J\in{\bf J}$, $b_J$ is supported in $3J$; \item we have \begin{equation} \sum_{J \in{\bf J}} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}; \end{equation} \item the ``good part'' $g$ satisfies \begin{equation} \|g\|_{L^2}^2 \lesssim \|f\|_{L^1} \sqrt{N} \lambda; \end{equation} \item the cubes $J$ satisfy \begin{equation} \|f\|_{L^1(J)} \lesssim |J|\lambda N^{-\frac{1}{2}} , \quad \|f-b_J\|_{L^2(J)} \lesssim \sqrt{|J|} \lambda; \end{equation} \item we have cancellation for all the frequencies of $\Theta$: for all $j=1,...,N$ and $J\in{\bf J}$, $\widehat{b_J}(\xi_j)=0$. \end{itemize} We aim to estimate the measure of the level-set $$ \Upsilon_\lambda:=\left\{x, |T(f)(x)|>\lambda\right\}.$$ With $b=\sum_J b_J$, we have \begin{align*} |\Upsilon_\lambda| & \leq \left|\left\{x, |T(g)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right| + \left|\left\{x, |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right| \\ & \lesssim \lambda^{-2} \|T(g)\|_{L^2}^2 + \left|\left\{x, |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right| \\ & \lesssim \lambda^{-1}\sqrt{N}\|f\|_{L^1} + \left|\left\{x, |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right|, \end{align*} where we used the $L^2$-boundedness of $T$. So it remains us to study the last term. Since (\ref{eq:sumJ}), we get $$ \left| \bigcup_{J\in {\bf J}} 4J \right| \lesssim \sum_{J} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}.$$ Consequently, it only remains to estimate the measure of the set $$ O_\lambda:= \left\{x \in \left(\bigcup_{J\in {\bf J}} 4J\right)^{c}, \quad |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}.$$ Since \begin{equation} |O_\lambda| \lesssim \lambda^{-1} \sum_{J} \|T(b_J)\|_{L^1((2J)^c)}, \end{equation} it is sufficient to estimate the $L^1$-norms. Consider $K$ the kernel of $T$ and a point $x_0\in \left(\bigcup_{J\in {\bf J}} 4J\right)^{c}$. Then, we can use the integral representation and we have $$ T(b)(x_0) = \int K(x_0,y) b(y) dy = \sum_{J} \int_{3J} K(x_0,y) b_J(y) dy.$$ To each $J$, we aim to take advantage of the cancellation properties of $b_J$, so we subtract the projection of $\left[y\to K(x_0,y)\right]$ on the space, spanned by $(e^{iy\cdot\eta})_{\eta\in \Theta}$. So we have \begin{align*} T(b)(x_0) & = \sum_{J}\sum_{j=1}^N \int_{3J} \left[K_j(x_0,y) - e^{i\xi_j \cdot c(J)} K_j(x_0,c(J))e^{-i\xi_j \cdot y}\right] b_J(y) dy \\ & = \sum_{J}\sum_{j=1}^N \int_{3J} \left[\widetilde{K}_{j}(x_0,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(x_0,c(J))\right]e^{i\xi_j\cdot (x_0-y)} b_J(y) dy \end{align*} where $c(J)$ is the center of $J$ and $\widetilde{K}_j(x,y):=K_j(x,y)e^{-i\xi_j \cdot (x-y)}$. We then write $$ T_j(b)(x_0) := \int \left[\widetilde{K}_{j}(x_0,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(x_0,c(J))\right]e^{i\xi_j \cdot (x_0-y)} b(y) dy.$$ such that $T(b) =\sum_j T_j(b)$. Due to the regularity assumption on $K$ (and so on $\widetilde{K}_j$), it comes for $y\in J$ and $x_0\in (2J)^c$ \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^N \left|\widetilde{K}_{j}(x_0,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(x_0,c(J))\right| \lesssim \frac{r_J}{|x_0-y|^{n+1}}. \end{equation} So we have $$ \|T(b_J)\|_{L^1((2J)^c)} \lesssim \iint_{|x-y|\geq r_J} \frac{r_J}{|x-y|^{n+1}} |b_J(y)| dxdy \lesssim \|b_J\|_{L^1} \lesssim |J| \lambda.$$ Finally, we obtain with (\ref{eq:Olambda}) that $$ |O_\lambda| \lesssim \sum_{J} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}, $$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition, handle the good part by $L^2$-boundedness, and use the frequency cancellation of $b_J$ against modulated-kernel differences for the bad part.
nodes.section: 2 Unweighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Apply the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition
nodes.statement: Consider $f$ a function in $L^1$ and $\lambda>0$, we use the Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition\footnote{In \cite{NOT}, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition is only described in $\R$. The proof is a combination of Lemma \ref{lem} and the usual Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition. Since both of them can be extended in a multi-dimensional framework, the multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund decomposition performed in \cite{NOT} still holds in $\R^n$.} of \cite{NOT} related to the collection of frequencies $\Theta$. So the function $f$ can be decomposed $f = g + \sum_{J\in {\bf J}} b_J$ with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item ${\bf J}$ is a collection of balls and $(3J)_{J\in{\bf J}}$ has a bounded overlap; \item for each $J\in{\bf J}$, $b_J$ is supported in $3J$; \item we have \begin{equation} \sum_{J \in{\bf J}} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}; \end{equation} \item the ``good part'' $g$ satisfies \begin{equation} \|g\|_{L^2}^2 \lesssim \|f\|_{L^1} \sqrt{N} \lambda; \end{equation} \item the cubes $J$ satisfy \begin{equation} \|f\|_{L^1(J)} \lesssim |J|\lambda N^{-\frac{1}{2}} , \quad \|f-b_J\|_{L^2(J)} \lesssim \sqrt{|J|} \lambda; \end{equation} \item we have cancellation for all the frequencies of $\Theta$: for all $j=1,...,N$ and $J\in{\bf J}$, $\widehat{b_J}(\xi_j)=0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Set up the good/bad splitting of $f$ at height $\lambda$ with its $\sqrt{N}$ bounds and frequency cancellation.
nodes.section: 2 Unweighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Split the level set and bound the good part
nodes.statement: We aim to estimate the measure of the level-set $$ \Upsilon_\lambda:=\left\{x, |T(f)(x)|>\lambda\right\}.$$ With $b=\sum_J b_J$, we have \begin{align*} |\Upsilon_\lambda| & \leq \left|\left\{x, |T(g)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right| + \left|\left\{x, |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right| \\ & \lesssim \lambda^{-2} \|T(g)\|_{L^2}^2 + \left|\left\{x, |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right| \\ & \lesssim \lambda^{-1}\sqrt{N}\|f\|_{L^1} + \left|\left\{x, |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}\right|, \end{align*} where we used the $L^2$-boundedness of $T$. So it remains us to study the last term.
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev plus the $L^2$-boundedness of $T$ dispose of the good part, leaving the bad part.
nodes.section: 2 Unweighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Discard the union of the dilated balls
nodes.statement: Since (\ref{eq:sumJ}), we get $$ \left| \bigcup_{J\in {\bf J}} 4J \right| \lesssim \sum_{J} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}.$$ Consequently, it only remains to estimate the measure of the set $$ O_\lambda:= \left\{x \in \left(\bigcup_{J\in {\bf J}} 4J\right)^{c}, \quad |T(b)(x)|>\lambda/2\right\}.$$ Since \begin{equation} |O_\lambda| \lesssim \lambda^{-1} \sum_{J} \|T(b_J)\|_{L^1((2J)^c)}, \end{equation} it is sufficient to estimate the $L^1$-norms.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the off-diagonal set $O_\lambda$ and to $L^1$-norms of $T(b_J)$ away from $2J$.
nodes.section: 2 Unweighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Subtract the modulated-kernel projection to exploit cancellation
nodes.statement: Consider $K$ the kernel of $T$ and a point $x_0\in \left(\bigcup_{J\in {\bf J}} 4J\right)^{c}$. Then, we can use the integral representation and we have $$ T(b)(x_0) = \int K(x_0,y) b(y) dy = \sum_{J} \int_{3J} K(x_0,y) b_J(y) dy.$$ To each $J$, we aim to take advantage of the cancellation properties of $b_J$, so we subtract the projection of $\left[y\to K(x_0,y)\right]$ on the space, spanned by $(e^{iy\cdot\eta})_{\eta\in \Theta}$. So we have \begin{align*} T(b)(x_0) & = \sum_{J}\sum_{j=1}^N \int_{3J} \left[K_j(x_0,y) - e^{i\xi_j \cdot c(J)} K_j(x_0,c(J))e^{-i\xi_j \cdot y}\right] b_J(y) dy \\ & = \sum_{J}\sum_{j=1}^N \int_{3J} \left[\widetilde{K}_{j}(x_0,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(x_0,c(J))\right]e^{i\xi_j\cdot (x_0-y)} b_J(y) dy \end{align*} where $c(J)$ is the center of $J$ and $\widetilde{K}_j(x,y):=K_j(x,y)e^{-i\xi_j \cdot (x-y)}$. We then write $$ T_j(b)(x_0) := \int \left[\widetilde{K}_{j}(x_0,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(x_0,c(J))\right]e^{i\xi_j \cdot (x_0-y)} b(y) dy.$$ such that $T(b) =\sum_j T_j(b)$. Due to the regularity assumption on $K$ (and so on $\widetilde{K}_j$), it comes for $y\in J$ and $x_0\in (2J)^c$ \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^N \left|\widetilde{K}_{j}(x_0,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(x_0,c(J))\right| \lesssim \frac{r_J}{|x_0-y|^{n+1}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use the vanishing of $\widehat{b_J}$ at each $\xi_j$ to replace $K_j$ by the difference of demodulated kernels, then invoke kernel regularity.

nodes.name: Conclude with the $L^1$ bound on the bad part
nodes.statement: So we have $$ \|T(b_J)\|_{L^1((2J)^c)} \lesssim \iint_{|x-y|\geq r_J} \frac{r_J}{|x-y|^{n+1}} |b_J(y)| dxdy \lesssim \|b_J\|_{L^1} \lesssim |J| \lambda.$$ Finally, we obtain with (\ref{eq:Olambda}) that $$ |O_\lambda| \lesssim \sum_{J} |J| \lesssim \sqrt{N} \|f\|_{L^1} \lambda^{-1}, $$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the kernel-difference bound to get $\||O_\lambda|\lesssim\sqrt{N}\|f\|_{L^1}\lambda^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Optimality of the order $N^{1/2}$ for the weak-$L^1$ estimate
nodes.statement: Following \cite{NOT}, the bound of order $N^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is optimal for the multi-frequency decomposition and for the weak-$L^1$ estimate.
nodes.section: 2 Unweighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Multi-frequency maximal sharp function $\M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp$
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies and $s\in[1,\infty)$. Consider a ball $Q$, we denote by $\pr_{\Theta,Q}$ the projection operator (in the $L^s$-sense) on the subspace of $L^s(3Q)$, spanned by $(\exp {i\xi\cdot})_{\xi\in \Theta}$. Let us specify this projection operator: consider $E$ the finite dimensional sub-space of $L^s(3Q)$, spanned by $(e^{i\xi\cdot})_{\xi\in \Theta}$ and equipped with the $L^s(3Q)$-norm. Since $E$ is of finite dimension, then for every $f\in L^s(Q)$ there exists $v:=\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f)\in E$ such that $$ \|f-v\|_{L^s(3Q)} = \inf_{\phi\in E} \|f-\phi\|_{L^s(3Q)}.$$ This projection operator may depend on $s$, which is not important for our purpose so this is implicit in the notation and we forget it. \mb Since $0\in E$, we obviously have \begin{equation} \|\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f)\|_{L^s(3Q)} \leq 2\|f\|_{L^s(Q)}. \end{equation} Then, we may define the maximal sharp function $$ \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (f)(x_0) := \sup_{x_0\in Q} \left(\aver{Q} \left|f-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f{\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Replace the ball average by the best $L^s$-approximation from the span of the exponentials $e^{i\xi\cdot}$, $\xi\in\Theta$, and take the sup over balls.
differentia: we denote by $\pr_{\Theta,Q}$ the projection operator (in the $L^s$-sense) on the subspace of $L^s(3Q)$, spanned by $(\exp {i\xi\cdot})_{\xi\in \Theta}$

nodes.name: Recovering the usual sharp maximal function and the Fefferman-Stein inequality
nodes.statement: Note that the usual sharp maximal function is the one obtained for $\Theta:=\{0\}$ and in this situation it is well-known that the maximal sharp function satisfies a so-called Fefferman-Stein inequality (see \cite{FS}).
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Fefferman-Stein inequality for the multi-frequency maximal sharp function
nodes.statement: Let $s\in(1,\infty)$, $t\in[1,\infty)$ and $p \in(s,\infty)$ be fixed. Then for every function $f\in L^s$ and every weight $\omega\in RH_{t'}$, we have for every $p\geq s$ $$ \|f\|_{L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{s}\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left\| \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp(f) \right\|_{L^p(\omega)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The weighted $L^p$ norm of $f$ is controlled by that of its multi-frequency sharp maximal function, at the cost of a power of $N$.
conclusions: $$ \|f\|_{L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{s}\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left\| \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp(f) \right\|_{L^p(\omega)}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Proof of the multi-frequency Fefferman-Stein inequality
nodes.statement: We make use on the abstract theory developed in \cite{AM} by Auscher and Martell. We also follow notations of \cite[Theorem 3.1]{AM}. Indeed, for each ball $Q\subset \rn$ we have the following $$ F(x) := |f(x)|^s \lesssim \left|f(x)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f{\bf 1}_Q)(x) \right|^s + \left|\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f{\bf 1}_Q)(x) \right|^s := G_Q(x)+H_Q(x). $$ By definition, it comes $$ \aver{Q} G_Q dx \leq \inf _{Q} \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (f)^s$$ and following Lemma \ref{lem} (with (\ref{eq:projection})) \begin{align*} \sup_{x\in Q} H_Q & = \|\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f {\bf 1}_Q)\|_{L^\infty(Q)}^s \lesssim N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left( \aver{3Q} |\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f {\bf 1}_Q)|^s dx\right) \\ & \lesssim N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left( \aver{Q} |f|^s dx\right) \lesssim N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \inf_Q {\mathcal M} F. \end{align*} So we can apply \cite[Theorem 3.1]{AM} (with $q=\infty$ and $a\simeq N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}}$) and by checking the behaviour of the constants with respect to ``$a$" in its proof, we obtain for every $p\geq 1$ $$ \left\| {\mathcal M}_s(f)^s \right\|_{L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{spt \max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left\| \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (f)^s \right\|_{L^p(\omega)},$$ which yields the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Split $|f|^s$ into a sharp-maximal part and a projection part, bound the latter by Lemma \ref{lem}, and feed the good-lambda machinery of Auscher-Martell.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Split $|f|^s$ into $G_Q + H_Q$
nodes.statement: We make use on the abstract theory developed in \cite{AM} by Auscher and Martell. We also follow notations of \cite[Theorem 3.1]{AM}. Indeed, for each ball $Q\subset \rn$ we have the following $$ F(x) := |f(x)|^s \lesssim \left|f(x)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f{\bf 1}_Q)(x) \right|^s + \left|\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f{\bf 1}_Q)(x) \right|^s := G_Q(x)+H_Q(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Set up the Auscher-Martell good-lambda framework with the oscillation/projection splitting on each ball.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Bound the average of $G_Q$ by the sharp maximal function
nodes.statement: By definition, it comes $$ \aver{Q} G_Q dx \leq \inf _{Q} \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (f)^s$$
nodes.statement_short: The oscillation part is dominated by the infimum over $Q$ of the multi-frequency sharp maximal function.

nodes.name: Bound $\sup_Q H_Q$ via the Nikolskii-type lemma
nodes.statement: and following Lemma \ref{lem} (with (\ref{eq:projection})) \begin{align*} \sup_{x\in Q} H_Q & = \|\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f {\bf 1}_Q)\|_{L^\infty(Q)}^s \lesssim N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left( \aver{3Q} |\pr_{\Theta,Q}(f {\bf 1}_Q)|^s dx\right) \\ & \lesssim N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left( \aver{Q} |f|^s dx\right) \lesssim N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \inf_Q {\mathcal M} F. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma \ref{lem} and the projection bound to control the projection part by $N^{s\max\{1/2,1/s\}}\inf_Q\M F$.

nodes.name: Apply Auscher-Martell Theorem 3.1 tracking the constant
nodes.statement: So we can apply \cite[Theorem 3.1]{AM} (with $q=\infty$ and $a\simeq N^{s\max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}}$) and by checking the behaviour of the constants with respect to ``$a$" in its proof, we obtain for every $p\geq 1$ $$ \left\| {\mathcal M}_s(f)^s \right\|_{L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{spt \max\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{s}\}} \left\| \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (f)^s \right\|_{L^p(\omega)},$$ which yields the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke the abstract good-lambda theorem with $a\simeq N^{s\max\{1/2,1/s\}}$ and track its dependence on $a$ to conclude.

nodes.name: Pointwise sharp-maximal estimate for $T$
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a Calder\'on-Zygmund operator relatively to $\Theta$ and $s\in(1,\infty)$. Then, we have the following pointwise estimate: $$ \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (T(f)) \lesssim N^{|\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{2}|} {\mathcal M}_s(f) .$$
nodes.statement_short: The multi-frequency sharp maximal function of $T(f)$ is pointwise dominated by $N^{|1/s-1/2|}\M_s(f)$.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a Calder\'on-Zygmund operator relatively to $\Theta$ and $s\in(1,\infty)$
conclusions: $$ \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp (T(f)) \lesssim N^{|\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{2}|} {\mathcal M}_s(f) .$$

nodes.name: Proof of the pointwise sharp-maximal estimate
nodes.statement: We follow the well-known proof for usual Calder\'on-Zygmund operators and adapt the arguments to the current situation. So consider a point $x_0$ and a ball $Q\subset \rn$ containing $x_0$, we have to estimate $$ \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}.$$ We split the function into a local part $f_0$ and an off-diagonal part $f_\infty$: $$f=f_0+f_\infty:= f{\bf 1}_{10 Q} + f {\bf 1}_{(10 Q)^c}.$$ By definition of the projection operator, we know that \begin{align*} \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} & \leq \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f_\infty){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} \\ & \leq \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_0) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} + \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_\infty)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f_\infty){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}. \end{align*} For the local part, we use boundedness in $L^s$ of the operator $T$ (Proposition \ref{prop:bound}), hence \begin{align*} \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_0)\right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} & \lesssim |Q|^{-\frac{1}{s}} \|T(f_0)\|_{L^s(Q)} \lesssim N^{(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s})} \left(|Q|^{-\frac{1}{s}} \|f_0\|_{L^s}\right) \\ & \lesssim N^{|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}|} {\mathcal M}_s(f)(x_0). \end{align*} Then let us focus on the second part, involving $f_\infty$. \\ We use the decomposition (with an integral representation) since we are in the off-diagonal case: for $x\in Q$ $$ T(f_\infty)(x) = \sum_{j=1}^N \int K_j(x,y) f_\infty(y) dy.$$ Consider the following function, defined on $3Q$ by (where $c(Q)$ is the center of $Q$) $$ \Phi:= x\in 3Q \rightarrow \sum_{j=1}^N \int e^{i\xi_j\cdot (x-c(Q))} K_j(c(Q),y) f_\infty(y) dy.$$ So $\Phi \in E$ (see Definition \ref{def:max}) and hence \begin{equation} \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_\infty)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f_\infty){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} \leq \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_\infty)-\Phi \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}. \end{equation} If we set $\widetilde{K}_j(x,z):=K_j(x,z)e^{-i\xi_j\cdot (x-z)}$, then $$ T(f_\infty)(x) -\Phi(x) = \sum_j \int \left[\widetilde{K}_{j}(x,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(c(Q),y)\right] e^{i\xi_j(x-y)} f_\infty(y) dy.$$ From the regularity assumption on the kernels $K_j$'s, we have for $y\in (10 Q)^c$ \begin{equation} \sum_{j} \left| \widetilde{K}_{j}(x,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(c(Q),y) \right| \lesssim r_Q \sup_{z\in Q} \sum_j \left| \nabla_{x} \widetilde{K}_{j}(z,y)\right| \lesssim r_Q^{-n}\left(1+\frac{d(y,Q)}{r_Q}\right)^{-n-1}. \end{equation} We also have (since $y\in (10 Q)^c$ and $x,c(Q)\in Q$) \begin{align*} \left| T(f_\infty)(x) -\Phi(x)\right| & \lesssim \int_{|z|\geq 10 r_Q} r_Q^{-n}\left(1+\frac{|x-c(Q)-z|}{r_Q}\right)^{-n-1} |f(c(Q)+z)| dz \\ & \lesssim \int_{|z|\geq 5 r_Q} r_Q^{-n}\left(1+\frac{|z|}{r_Q}\right)^{-n-1} |f(x_0+z)| dz \\ & \lesssim {\mathcal M}(f)(x_0), \end{align*} which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Split $f$ into local and off-diagonal parts: the local part is handled by the $L^s$-boundedness of $T$, the off-diagonal part by subtracting the explicit element $\Phi\in E$ and using kernel regularity.

nodes.name: Fix a ball and reduce to the local oscillation average
nodes.statement: We follow the well-known proof for usual Calder\'on-Zygmund operators and adapt the arguments to the current situation. So consider a point $x_0$ and a ball $Q\subset \rn$ containing $x_0$, we have to estimate $$ \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Fix $x_0\in Q$ and reduce to bounding the $L^s$ oscillation of $T(f)$ against its projection.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Split into local and off-diagonal parts
nodes.statement: We split the function into a local part $f_0$ and an off-diagonal part $f_\infty$: $$f=f_0+f_\infty:= f{\bf 1}_{10 Q} + f {\bf 1}_{(10 Q)^c}.$$ By definition of the projection operator, we know that \begin{align*} \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} & \leq \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f_\infty){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} \\ & \leq \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_0) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} + \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_\infty)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f_\infty){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $f=f{\bf 1}_{10Q}+f{\bf 1}_{(10Q)^c}$ and use minimality of the projection to split the oscillation into two terms.

nodes.name: Bound the local part by the $L^s$-boundedness of $T$
nodes.statement: For the local part, we use boundedness in $L^s$ of the operator $T$ (Proposition \ref{prop:bound}), hence \begin{align*} \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_0)\right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} & \lesssim |Q|^{-\frac{1}{s}} \|T(f_0)\|_{L^s(Q)} \lesssim N^{(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s})} \left(|Q|^{-\frac{1}{s}} \|f_0\|_{L^s}\right) \\ & \lesssim N^{|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}|} {\mathcal M}_s(f)(x_0). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $L^s$ bound of Proposition \ref{prop:bound} to $f_0$ and majorize by $N^{|1/2-1/s|}\M_s(f)(x_0)$.

nodes.name: Construct the comparison function $\Phi \in E$
nodes.statement: Then let us focus on the second part, involving $f_\infty$. \\ We use the decomposition (with an integral representation) since we are in the off-diagonal case: for $x\in Q$ $$ T(f_\infty)(x) = \sum_{j=1}^N \int K_j(x,y) f_\infty(y) dy.$$ Consider the following function, defined on $3Q$ by (where $c(Q)$ is the center of $Q$) $$ \Phi:= x\in 3Q \rightarrow \sum_{j=1}^N \int e^{i\xi_j\cdot (x-c(Q))} K_j(c(Q),y) f_\infty(y) dy.$$ So $\Phi \in E$ (see Definition \ref{def:max}) and hence \begin{equation} \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_\infty)-\pr_{\Theta,Q}(T(f_\infty){\bf 1}_Q) \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}} \leq \left( \aver{Q} \left|T(f_\infty)-\Phi \right|^s dx \right)^{\frac{1}{s}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Freeze the kernel at $c(Q)$ to build an explicit exponential sum $\Phi\in E$, which majorizes the projection error.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Kernel regularity estimate for the demodulated kernels
nodes.statement: If we set $\widetilde{K}_j(x,z):=K_j(x,z)e^{-i\xi_j\cdot (x-z)}$, then $$ T(f_\infty)(x) -\Phi(x) = \sum_j \int \left[\widetilde{K}_{j}(x,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(c(Q),y)\right] e^{i\xi_j(x-y)} f_\infty(y) dy.$$ From the regularity assumption on the kernels $K_j$'s, we have for $y\in (10 Q)^c$ \begin{equation} \sum_{j} \left| \widetilde{K}_{j}(x,y) - \widetilde{K}_j(c(Q),y) \right| \lesssim r_Q \sup_{z\in Q} \sum_j \left| \nabla_{x} \widetilde{K}_{j}(z,y)\right| \lesssim r_Q^{-n}\left(1+\frac{d(y,Q)}{r_Q}\right)^{-n-1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Express $T(f_\infty)-\Phi$ through demodulated kernel differences and bound them by the standard H\"older-type decay.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Conclude by the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function
nodes.statement: We also have (since $y\in (10 Q)^c$ and $x,c(Q)\in Q$) \begin{align*} \left| T(f_\infty)(x) -\Phi(x)\right| & \lesssim \int_{|z|\geq 10 r_Q} r_Q^{-n}\left(1+\frac{|x-c(Q)-z|}{r_Q}\right)^{-n-1} |f(c(Q)+z)| dz \\ & \lesssim \int_{|z|\geq 5 r_Q} r_Q^{-n}\left(1+\frac{|z|}{r_Q}\right)^{-n-1} |f(x_0+z)| dz \\ & \lesssim {\mathcal M}(f)(x_0), \end{align*} which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the decaying kernel against $|f|$ to obtain a bound by $\M(f)(x_0)$.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Weighted boundedness of $T$ for $p>s\geq 2$
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies. For $p\in (2,\infty)$, $s\in[2,p)$ and $t\in(1,\infty)$, a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator $T$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ for every weight $\omega \in RH_{t'} \cap {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$ with $$ \|T\|_{L^p(\omega) \to L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{2s}+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: For $p>s\geq 2$ the weighted operator norm is $O(N^{tp/(2s)+(1/2-1/s)})$.
assumptions: Let $\Theta$ be a collection of $N$ frequencies
conclusions: a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator $T$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$
$$ \|T\|_{L^p(\omega) \to L^p(\omega)} \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{2s}+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right)}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Proof of the weighted boundedness corollary
nodes.statement: Using Propositions \ref{prop:FeffermanStein} and \ref{prop:maximal}, it follows that for $p>s\geq 2$ (assuming $\omega \in {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$) \begin{align*} \|T(f) \|_{L^p(\omega)} & \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{2s}} \left\| \M_{s,\Theta}^\sharp [T(f)] \right\|_{L^p(\omega)} \\ & \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{2s}+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right)} \left\| {\mathcal M}_s(f) \right\|_{L^p(\omega)} \\ & \lesssim N^{\frac{tp}{2s}+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right)} \left\| f \right\|_{L^p(\omega)}, \end{align*} where we used weighted boundedness of the maximal function since $\omega \in {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the Fefferman-Stein inequality, the pointwise sharp-maximal estimate, and the ${\mathbb A}_{p/s}$-boundedness of $\M_s$.
nodes.section: 3 Weighted estimates for multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operators

nodes.name: Bounded open set $\Omega$ with $(n-1)$-dimensional boundary
nodes.statement: Consider also $\Omega$ a bounded open subset of $\rn$ such that its boundary $\Gamma:=\overline{\Omega}\setminus \Omega$ is an hyper-manifold of Hausdorff dimension $n-1$.

nodes.name: Generalized Bochner-Riesz multiplier $R_{\Omega,\delta}$
nodes.statement: For $\delta>0$, we then define the generalized Bochner-Riesz multiplier, given by $$ R_{\Omega,\delta}(f) (x) := \int_\Omega e^{ix\cdot \xi} \widehat{f}(\xi) m_\delta d\xi,$$ where $m_\delta$ is a smooth symbol supported in $\overline{\Omega}$ and satisfying in $\Omega$ $$ | \partial^\alpha m_\delta(\xi)| \lesssim d(\xi,\Gamma)^{\delta-|\alpha|}.$$
nodes.statement_short: A Fourier multiplier supported in $\overline{\Omega}$ whose symbol degenerates like $d(\xi,\Gamma)^\delta$ at the boundary.
differentia: $m_\delta$ is a smooth symbol supported in $\overline{\Omega}$

nodes.name: Whitney covering of $\Omega$
nodes.statement: We first use a Whitney covering $(O_i)_i$ of $\Omega$. That is a collection of sub-balls such that \begin{itemize} \item the collection $(O_i)_i$ covers $\Omega$ and has a bounded overlap; \item the radius $r_{O_i}$ is equivalent to $d(O_i,\Gamma)$. \end{itemize}
differentia: the collection $(O_i)_i$ covers $\Omega$ and has a bounded overlap

nodes.name: Partition of the unity $(\chi_i)_i$ adapted to the Whitney covering
nodes.statement: Associated to this collection, we build a partition of the unity $(\chi_i)_i$ of smooth functions such that $\chi_i$ is supported on $O_i$ with $$ \sum_i \chi_i(\xi) = {\bf 1}_{\Omega}(\xi)$$ and $\|\partial^\alpha \chi_i\|_\infty \lesssim r_{O_i}^{-|\alpha|}$.

nodes.name: Scale decomposition of $R_\delta$ into the operators $T_j = 2^{j\delta} U_j$
nodes.statement: Then, $R_{\delta}$ may be written as $$ R_{\delta}(f) (x) = \sum_{j=-\infty}^\infty T_j(f)(x),$$ with \begin{align} T_j(f)(x) & :=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{l,}{2^j \leq r_{O_l}< 2^{j+1}}} \int_\Omega e^{ix\cdot \xi} \widehat{f}(\xi) m_\delta(\xi) \chi_l(\xi) d\xi \nonumber \\ & =2^{j\delta} U_j(f)(x), \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Group the Whitney pieces by dyadic radius $2^j$, factoring out the boundary decay $2^{j\delta}$.

nodes.name: Normalized dyadic piece $U_j$
nodes.statement: where we set $$ U_j(f)(x):= \sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{l,}{2^j \leq r_{O_l}< 2^{j+1}}} \int_\Omega e^{ix\cdot \xi} \widehat{f}(\xi) (2^{-j\delta} m_\delta(\xi)) \chi_l(\xi) d\xi.$$

nodes.name: Observation: $U_j$ is a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator
nodes.statement: {\bf Observation :} The main idea is to observe that the operator $U_j$ is a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator associated to the collection $$ \Theta_j :=\{ c(O_l), \ 2^j \leq r_{O_l}< 2^{j+1} \} \qquad \textrm{with} \qquad \sharp \Theta_j \simeq 2^{-j(n-1)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Each single-scale piece $U_j$ is a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator over the $\simeq 2^{-j(n-1)}$ Whitney centers at scale $2^j$.
conclusions: The main idea is to observe that the operator $U_j$ is a multi-frequency Calder\'on-Zygmund operator associated to the collection $$ \Theta_j :=\{ c(O_l), \ 2^j \leq r_{O_l}< 2^{j+1} \} \qquad \textrm{with} \qquad \sharp \Theta_j \simeq 2^{-j(n-1)}.$$

nodes.name: Kernel $L^1$-bound and weighted boundedness of $U_j$
nodes.statement: Uniformly with $j\lesssim 0$, the multiplier $U_j$ is a convolution operation with a kernel $K_j$ satisfying $$ \|K_j\|_{L^1} \lesssim 2^{-j \frac{n-1}{2}}.$$ Hence, it follows that $U_j$ is bounded on Lebesgue space $L^p$ for every $p\in[1,\infty]$. Moreover for every $s\in[1,2]$, $p\in(s,\infty)$ and every weight $\omega\in {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$, $U_j$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ with $$ \| U_j\|_{L^p(\omega) \rightarrow L^p(\omega)} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{s}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The single-scale kernel has $L^1$ norm $O(2^{-j(n-1)/2})$, giving $L^p$ bounds for all $p$ and weighted bounds of order $2^{-j(n-1)/s}$.
assumptions: for every $s\in[1,2]$, $p\in(s,\infty)$ and every weight $\omega\in {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$
conclusions: the multiplier $U_j$ is a convolution operation with a kernel $K_j$ satisfying $$ \|K_j\|_{L^1} \lesssim 2^{-j \frac{n-1}{2}}.$$
$U_j$ is bounded on Lebesgue space $L^p$ for every $p\in[1,\infty]$
$U_j$ is bounded on $L^p(\omega)$ with $$ \| U_j\|_{L^p(\omega) \rightarrow L^p(\omega)} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{s}}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of the kernel and weighted bounds for $U_j$
nodes.statement: The operator $U_j$ is a Fourier multiplier, associated to the symbol $$\sigma_j(\xi):=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{l,}{2^j \leq r_{O_l}< 2^{j+1}}} (2^{-j\delta} m_\delta(\xi)) \chi_l(\xi).$$ Since the considered balls $(O_l)_l$ are almost disjoint, it comes that $$ \|\sigma_j\|_{L^2} \lesssim |\{\xi, d(\xi,\partial \Omega)\simeq 2^j \}|^{\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim 2^{\frac{j}{2}}.$$ Moreover, using regularity assumptions on $m_\delta$, we deduce that for every $\alpha$ $$ \|\partial^\alpha \sigma_j\|_{L^2} \lesssim 2^{-j|\alpha|} |\{\xi, d(\xi,\partial \Omega) \simeq 2^j \}|^{\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim 2^{j(\frac{1}{2}-|\alpha|)}.$$ So with $K_j:= \mathcal{F}(\sigma_j)$, it follows that for any integer $M$ \begin{equation} \left\| (1+2^{j}|\cdot|)^{M} K_j\right\|_{L^2} \lesssim 2^{\frac{j}{2}}. \end{equation} Hence $$ \left\| K_j\right\|_{L^1} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{2}}.$$ Using Minkowski inequality, we deduce that for every $p\in[1,\infty]$ $$ \| U_j\|_{L^p \to L^p} \lesssim \|K_j\|_{L^1} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{2}}.$$ Let us now focus on the second claim about weighted estimates. Using integrations by parts for computing the kernel $K_j$, it comes for any integer $M$ \begin{equation} \left\| (1+2^{j}|\cdot|)^{M} K_j\right\|_{L^\infty} \lesssim 2^{j}. \end{equation} By interpolation with (\ref{eq:L^2}), for $s\in[1,2]$ we get \begin{equation} \left\| (1+2^{j}|\cdot|)^{M} K_j\right\|_{L^{s'}} \lesssim 2^{\frac{j}{s}}, \end{equation} which gives $$ U_j(f) \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{s}} \M_{s}(f).$$ Hence, for every $p> s$ and every weight $\omega \in {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$ $$ \|U_j\|_{L^p(\omega) \to L^p(\omega)} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{s}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Estimate the symbol and its derivatives in $L^2$, convert to weighted $L^2$/$L^\infty$ bounds on $K_j$, then interpolate to dominate $U_j$ pointwise by $\M_s$.

nodes.name: Identify the symbol $\sigma_j$ of $U_j$
nodes.statement: The operator $U_j$ is a Fourier multiplier, associated to the symbol $$\sigma_j(\xi):=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{l,}{2^j \leq r_{O_l}< 2^{j+1}}} (2^{-j\delta} m_\delta(\xi)) \chi_l(\xi).$$
nodes.statement_short: Write $U_j$ as a Fourier multiplier with the explicit single-scale symbol $\sigma_j$.

nodes.name: $L^2$ bounds on $\sigma_j$ and its derivatives
nodes.statement: Since the considered balls $(O_l)_l$ are almost disjoint, it comes that $$ \|\sigma_j\|_{L^2} \lesssim |\{\xi, d(\xi,\partial \Omega)\simeq 2^j \}|^{\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim 2^{\frac{j}{2}}.$$ Moreover, using regularity assumptions on $m_\delta$, we deduce that for every $\alpha$ $$ \|\partial^\alpha \sigma_j\|_{L^2} \lesssim 2^{-j|\alpha|} |\{\xi, d(\xi,\partial \Omega) \simeq 2^j \}|^{\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim 2^{j(\frac{1}{2}-|\alpha|)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Almost disjointness plus symbol regularity give $\|\partial^\alpha\sigma_j\|_{L^2}\lesssim 2^{j(1/2-|\alpha|)}$.

nodes.name: Weighted $L^2$ bound on the kernel and its $L^1$ norm
nodes.statement: So with $K_j:= \mathcal{F}(\sigma_j)$, it follows that for any integer $M$ \begin{equation} \left\| (1+2^{j}|\cdot|)^{M} K_j\right\|_{L^2} \lesssim 2^{\frac{j}{2}}. \end{equation} Hence $$ \left\| K_j\right\|_{L^1} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{2}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the symbol bounds to a weighted $L^2$ bound on $K_j$, whence $\|K_j\|_{L^1}\lesssim 2^{-j(n-1)/2}$.

nodes.name: Unweighted $L^p$ boundedness by Minkowski's inequality
nodes.statement: Using Minkowski inequality, we deduce that for every $p\in[1,\infty]$ $$ \| U_j\|_{L^p \to L^p} \lesssim \|K_j\|_{L^1} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{2}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Convolution with an $L^1$ kernel is bounded on every $L^p$.

nodes.name: $L^\infty$ bound on the weighted kernel
nodes.statement: Let us now focus on the second claim about weighted estimates. Using integrations by parts for computing the kernel $K_j$, it comes for any integer $M$ \begin{equation} \left\| (1+2^{j}|\cdot|)^{M} K_j\right\|_{L^\infty} \lesssim 2^{j}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts yields the companion $L^\infty$ bound on the weighted kernel.

nodes.name: Interpolate and conclude the weighted estimate
nodes.statement: By interpolation with (\ref{eq:L^2}), for $s\in[1,2]$ we get \begin{equation} \left\| (1+2^{j}|\cdot|)^{M} K_j\right\|_{L^{s'}} \lesssim 2^{\frac{j}{s}}, \end{equation} which gives $$ U_j(f) \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{s}} \M_{s}(f).$$ Hence, for every $p> s$ and every weight $\omega \in {\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$ $$ \|U_j\|_{L^p(\omega) \to L^p(\omega)} \lesssim 2^{-j\frac{n-1}{s}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate the $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ kernel bounds to dominate $U_j$ by $\M_s$, then use ${\mathbb A}_{p/s}$-boundedness of $\M_s$.

nodes.name: The single-scale bound beats the general corollary
nodes.statement: In this context, $\sharp \Theta_j \simeq 2^{-j(n-1)}$, so the constant $2^{-j \frac{n-1}{s}}$ is equivalent to $(\sharp \Theta_j)^{\frac{1}{s}}$ and this is a better constant than the one obtained in Corollary \ref{cor} (for a subclass of ${\mathbb A}_{\frac{p}{s}}$ weights). \\ So improving these ``easy bounds'' means to obtain inequalities such as $$ \| U_j\|_{L^p(\omega) \rightarrow L^p(\omega)} \lesssim (\sharp \Theta_j)^{\gamma}$$ for some better exponent $\gamma<\frac{1}{s}$.
nodes.statement_short: The easy single-scale bound is $(\sharp\Theta_j)^{1/s}$, better than the corollary's exponent, so progress means beating $\gamma=1/s$.

nodes.name: Curvature-improved Bochner-Riesz bounds for the unit ball
nodes.statement: for example for the unit ball (using its non vanishing curvature), we know that (see \cite{Lee, survey}) $$ \|U_j\|_{L^p\to L^p} \lesssim 2^{-j\delta(p)}$$ with if $n=2$ $$ \delta(p):= \max\left\{ 2\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}\right|-\frac{1}{2},0 \right\}.$$ and if $n\geq 3$ and $p\geq \frac{2(n+2)}{n}$ or $p\leq \frac{2(n+2)}{n+4}$ $$ \delta(p):= \max\left\{ n\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}\right|-\frac{1}{2},0 \right\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: For the ball, curvature improves the single-scale $L^p$ bound to $2^{-j\delta(p)}$ with the stated $\delta(p)$.
assumptions: for the unit ball (using its non vanishing curvature)
conclusions: $$ \|U_j\|_{L^p\to L^p} \lesssim 2^{-j\delta(p)}$$
nodes.origin_citation: Lee 2004; Tao, Recent progress on the restriction conjecture

nodes.name: Question: how to improve the exponent $\gamma$
nodes.statement: {\bf Question :} The general approach, developed in the previous section, only allows to get an exponent $$ \gamma=\frac{tp}{2s}+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{s}\right)$$ (with some $s\in[2,p)$) which is bigger than $\frac{1}{2}$ (since $p>s\geq 2$ and $t>1$). So to improve this exponent $\gamma$, two things seem to be crucial: \begin{itemize} \item to extend the use of Lemma \ref{lem} for $p\geq 2$ which would allow us to get an exponent $\frac{tp}{s^2}$ instead of $\frac{tp}{2s}$; \item to use the geometry of the boundary $\Gamma$ to get better exponents, even for the unweighted estimates. Indeed, for example for the unit ball (using its non vanishing curvature), we know that (see \cite{Lee, survey}) $$ \|U_j\|_{L^p\to L^p} \lesssim 2^{-j\delta(p)}$$ with if $n=2$ $$ \delta(p):= \max\left\{ 2\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}\right|-\frac{1}{2},0 \right\}.$$ and if $n\geq 3$ and $p\geq \frac{2(n+2)}{n}$ or $p\leq \frac{2(n+2)}{n+4}$ $$ \delta(p):= \max\left\{ n\left|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}\right|-\frac{1}{2},0 \right\}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Getting $\gamma$ below $1/2$ requires extending the Nikolskii lemma past $p=2$ and exploiting the curvature of $\Gamma$.
